# Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin

Mayank Rathee   Alexander Stepanov   Shalin Madabhavi Affiliation: UC
Berkeley   Foothill High School    Jinhao Zhu   Raluca Ada Popa   Ion
Stoica

###### Abstract

Coding agents have become increasingly long-horizon, autonomous, reliant
on general-purpose shell and maintain their own persistent memory for
self-improvement. While these capabilities have made the agents
powerful, they have also made them harder to defend against external
adversaries. Defenses that restrict this architecture—typed tools,
information-flow control, or policy prediction engines—give up too much
functionality to be adopted. Agents deployed today (e.g. Claude, Codex)
rely on a combination of user-mediated and auto-mode sandboxing as their
primary defense. In user-mediated sandboxing, user-maintained policies
decay over time and repeated permission requests cause user fatigue,
while auto mode’s tool-call classifiers learn no user-specific policy
and are not meant to defend against adversarial setups.

Pincer is a new defense that operates at the resource layer and works
alongside existing defenses at the tool-call layer like the auto mode.
At the core of Pincer lies a _digital twin_, an isolated-context model
that automatically learns and enforces dynamic user-specific
least-privilege policies. The digital twin keeps continually learning
the user’s preferences allowing it to act as the user’s proxy for the
agent’s permission requests.

To emulate the learning phase, we propose a new user-centric dataset
with examples following a multi-day transcript of user-agent
interaction. Our evaluation shows that Pincer performs strongly on both
security and utility in comparison to several baselines which includes
variants of LLM judges and adaptations of Conseca (HotOS ’25). We
highlight attack types where Pincer’s design leads to a significant
security improvement compared to all other baselines, while
outperforming the baselines even for other types of attacks.

## 1 Introduction

Coding agents \[[3](#bib.bib3), [42](#bib.bib42), [43](#bib.bib43),
[40](#bib.bib40)\] have become increasingly autonomous, memory-driven,
and reliant on general purpose computer-use tools like shell. These
capabilities have ushered in a new era of computing with powerful
automation, while also opening the door for vulnerabilities and
attackers \[[41](#bib.bib41), [5](#bib.bib5), [55](#bib.bib55),
[27](#bib.bib27), [24](#bib.bib24)\]. Researchers in both academia and
industry have been looking for ways to make agents safer while balancing
their usefulness.

In academia, there has been a major push towards strong defenses that in
turn heavily restrict the agent’s capabilities \[[32](#bib.bib32),
[14](#bib.bib14), [13](#bib.bib13), [21](#bib.bib21), [48](#bib.bib48),
[53](#bib.bib53), [56](#bib.bib56)\]. On the other hand, the focus in
industry has been towards defenses that work well for most day-to-day
use and preserving the functionality of agents as much as
possible \[[29](#bib.bib29), [4](#bib.bib4), [40](#bib.bib40),
[42](#bib.bib42), [3](#bib.bib3)\]. Sandboxed execution with policies
over the agent’s privileges, user-mediated permissions, and tool-call
classifiers define these defenses. However, their effectiveness tends to
decay over time (privilege creep and permission fatigue) and deviation
from production traffic, e.g. when an adversary wants to take over the
agent, can cause further failures \[[30](#bib.bib30)\]. In this work, we
focus primarily on deployed agents and their existing defenses.

We present a new defense that plugs directly into today’s agents and
targets the resource layer that sits behind tools; for example files,
web, etc. Central to our design is an entity we call the digital twin
that learns user behavior over time to automatically infer which
resources should be accessible to the agent for any given task. It
additionally provides defense-in-depth by staying compatible with
existing defenses that are already deployed. We call the system that
composes an off-the-shelf agent with our defense Pincer¹¹ 1 Since
pincers offer finer control than claws, we use Pincer as our system name
to differentiate from less safe agents like OpenClaw.. Our contributions
are as follows:

1.  1.  Pincer, an agentic system that learns user behavior and
        automatically authorizes resources for the agent on a per task
        basis.
2.  2.  A user-centric synthetic dataset containing a coherent set of
        examples from different users’ interaction with their agents over
        several days. The examples contain both attacks and benign
        workflows. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first dataset of
        this kind.
3.  3.  Implementation and evaluation of Pincer on top of a lightweight
        off-the-shelf agent NanoClaw \[[40](#bib.bib40)\].

### 1.1 Technical Overview

Deployed agents today run in a sandbox where a policy file, maintained
by the user, describes what privileges the agent gets within the sandbox
including tools it can use, whitelisted commands, and resources it can
access. Whenever the agent hits the wall of the sandbox, a permission
request is issued to the user specific to where the agent is stuck.
Given this user-mediated sandboxing, two challenges show up. First,
policies can become over-permissive over time as permissions accumulate
because users rarely revoke permissions they might have granted under a
deadline; this is known as privilege creep \[[18](#bib.bib18),
[4](#bib.bib4)\]. Secondly, repeated permission requests lead to
permission fatigue for the users causing their scrutiny to decrease over
time \[[19](#bib.bib19), [36](#bib.bib36)\]. In response to these
concerns, Anthropic released the auto mode \[[29](#bib.bib29)\] which is
a classifier that sits at the tool-call layer and resolves permission
requests to reduce user fatigue. While it works well for regular usage,
recent work on stress-testing found that it allows a majority of unsafe
operations to go through \[[30](#bib.bib30)\]. For example, directly
executing a dangerous command like rm -rf \* is blocked by the
classifier, but the same command can be embedded in a harmlessly named
Python file test.py, and the classifier allows python3 test.py to run.
This gives an adversary an easy way to bypass or fool the classifier. In
fact, it is not practical for any tool-call layer classifier to reason
through the effects of code, especially when the dangerous command is
buried deep in the dependency chain. The same holds even without code:
reasoning through the possible effects of a complex shell command at the
tool-call layer can be infeasible. Moreover, the classifier doesn’t
learn user-specific policies; if the classifier thinks git push is
dangerous while the user’s workflow deems it as no risk, the user has to
manually edit the policy file, otherwise the classifier will keep
blocking it. This is why the problem of privilege creep is left
unresolved by auto mode. We address these challenges in Pincer and
describe our design next.

#### Privilege creep and permission fatigue.

The primary cause of privilege creep is policies that don’t adapt over
time, go stale, and become over-permissive, while for permission
fatigue, it is the repeated user involvement. We address both of these
problems by automating the policy management as well as the permission
resolution via a large language model (LLM) based party called the
digital twin. Given a history of user behavior, the digital twin learns
the implicit user-specific policies, adapts them over time, and steps in
when the agent issues a permission request. As part of this design, we
have to answer two important questions: (1) where in the agentic
workflow the digital twin sits, which also defines the policies it can
enforce, and (2) how to prevent the digital twin from getting
compromised under attacks.

#### Resource layer instead of tool-call layer.

The digital twin sits at the resource layer instead of the tool-call
layer, i.e. it gates access to resources, not tools or commands. When
the agent makes a tool-call, it resolves to an underlying resource and
that is where an authorization from the digital twin is needed,
otherwise the tool call simply aborts. This has two clear advantages.
First, we side-step the generally intractable space of commands and tool
calls which prevents our enforcement from becoming ineffective and
collapsing under the size of the enforceable domain. A resource
decision, on the other hand, is over one concrete named object with a
small fixed set of access modes \[[51](#bib.bib51)\] (e.g. reading a
file directly through bash or via python or indirectly through imported
modules vs read/write for a file). Second, the number of tool calls is
typically significantly larger than the resources they operate over²² 2
Once access to a resource is granted, the access stays for the duration
of the task. Therefore, the number of resource requests from the agent
doesn’t necessarily grow with the task complexity unlike the tool
calls.. Therefore, the token cost of the digital twin is significantly
cheaper at the resource layer. Since the digital twin sits at the
resource layer, it only enforces policies over resources. The resource
layer enforcement doesn’t replace the need for tool-call layer
enforcement because the former is more coarse-grained; for example it
cannot tell if an accessed file is overwritten with contents of a
different accessed file. Due to this reason, a deployment should employ
defense-in-depth by using Pincer with compatible tool-call layer
defenses like the auto mode in Claude Code \[[29](#bib.bib29)\].

#### Defending the digital twin from attacks.

The digital twin is a model that can get compromised if it interacts
with untrusted content. Once compromised, it can grant unrestricted
access to the agent which can be catastrophic. To mitigate this
threat, Pincer provides architectural separation to the digital twin by
restricting the majority of its input to be only trusted - consisting of
tokens authorized by the user which includes the user prompts (current
and past), the permission requests granted by the user in the past, or
any additional tokens the user explicitly chooses to authorize. A
digital twin, however, has to accept a limited amount of information
that doesn’t originate from the user. The prime example of this is the
request itself which originates from the agent who may be under the
attacker’s control given its exposure to a myriad of untrusted
content. Pincer sanitizes this information before the twin (we refer to
the digital twin as “twin” going forward) sees it.
In [Section 5](#S5 "5 Pincer ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin"),
we go into detail on subtle ways an attacker can influence the twin’s
decision and how we close that gap.

#### Content-dependent policies.

The information our twin gets when making a resource decision doesn’t
include contents of the resource (e.g. file contents). This is by design
to protect it from getting compromised via untrusted resources
controlled by an attacker. However, due to this, content-based policies
(e.g. a file can only be read if it contains no secrets) cannot be
enforced. To address this limitation, we make the twin’s decision a
conjunction of a few votes, each serving a very specific function
(see [Section 5.6](#S5.SS6 "5.6 Pre-Committed Policies ‣ 5 Pincer ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")
for details). One of these votes is cast after seeing contents of the
requested resource. A vote based on untrusted file contents always risks
getting compromised and this is where the other votes come in; they are
isolated from free-form untrusted content.

## 2 System Architecture

![Refer to caption](2610.02569v1/agentic-arch.png)

Figure 1: The architecture today’s coding agents have converged on. An
LLM drives an autonomous loop over persistent memory and general-purpose
tools and acts on external resources, such as local files, the network,
and remote services, through those tools. The box encloses the
components under the agent’s own control; the user and the resources the
agent acts on sit outside it.

Agents deployed to millions of people today \[[42](#bib.bib42),
[43](#bib.bib43), [3](#bib.bib3)\] have all converged to a similar
high-level architecture as shown
in [Figure 1](#S2.F1 "In 2 System Architecture ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin").
The user sends in a prompt to the LLM that controls the agent. The LLM
references its memory and starts working on the user’s task. It has
access to a variety of tools and it uses them to execute the task. The
tools interact with resources like files or the web. The agent runs
inside a sandbox with a user-editable policy, and optionally a
classifier that adjudicates tool calls to reduce the permission burden
on the user whenever a tool call doesn’t find grounding in the
policy \[[29](#bib.bib29), [4](#bib.bib4)\]. As we mentioned before
in [Section 1](#S1 "1 Introduction ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin"),
with this design, agents run into the problems of privilege creep and
permission fatigue without the classifier, while the classifier doesn’t
learn user-specific policies and isn’t effective at making safe
decisions under atypical situations \[[30](#bib.bib30)\], for example
under attack. Importantly, the classifier addresses permission fatigue
but doesn’t resolve the privilege creep issue; for user-specific
policies, which may change from time to time, the user has to maintain
the policy file and define exceptions for the classifier.

### 2.1 Pincer’s Design

Our approach to address these challenges is to bolster the security of
the system at a deeper layer than handled by the classifier while
avoiding both privilege creep and permission fatigue. The layer we
bolster is the resource layer which sits deeper than the tool call
layer, but is also more coarse in its enforcement potential compared to
the tool call layer, and in deployment, agents should pair it with the
tool call classifier. To automatically learn user-specific policies and
prevent privilege creep, we introduce a digital twin who constantly
learns user preferences and enforces those policies automatically.

#### System components.

Our system has four classes of components:

- •
  LLMs: We have two separate LLMs as part of our system: the worker (the
  main LLM in the agent) and the twin (a type of LLM judge).
- •
  Special-purpose state: Any state directly maintained by each LLM. For
  example the memory maintained by the worker.
- •
  Tools: Tools used by the worker to perform a task. For example the
  shell tool. Our system has a special tool (the resource request tool)
  that allows the worker to talk to the twin via a narrow channel.
- •
  Resources: Any resources that tools access. For example: files, email,
  web, etc.

#### High-level system workflow.

The user provides a prompt describing the task. The worker performs the
task, while the twin is responsible for resource authorization for the
worker. Given the prompt, the worker accesses its special-purpose state
(a.k.a. the memory) and then calls tools to complete the task. The tools
access resources and if a resource isn’t authorized for the worker, it
uses a special resource-request tool to make a request for the said
resource to the twin. The twin analyzes the request and may decide to
grant or deny it. If granted, the worker-invoked tools can access the
resource.

## 3 Threat Model and System Goals

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 2: Our threat model.

Our threat model is summarized
in [Figure 2](#S3.F2 "In 3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")
and detailed below.

###### Definition 1 (Trusted party: the user).

A trusted party or object is one that is outside the adversary’s
control. A trusted party cannot be compromised by an adversary and any
actions produced by them are deemed trusted. The user is assumed to be a
trusted party.

#### The adversary.

The adversary can arbitrarily corrupt anything except trusted parties
and the trusted computing base (TCB). We consider a powerful adversary
who can arbitrarily corrupt the worker agent, any third-party tools that
the agent uses, and any of the resources (names as well as content). The
adversary cannot manipulate two channels: the communication channel from
the user to the system and the communication channel between the twin
and the model provider. The adversary cannot alter the system’s code and
cannot modify its behavior, and it doesn’t control the weights of ML
models used by the system.

#### Trusted Computing Base (TCB).

We consider the following as part of our TCB: First, the twin LLM, with
its weights and inference stack. Second, our system stack which includes
the resource request tool that allows the worker to issue requests to
the twin and Pincer’s write isolation for the twin’s special-purpose
state from any untrusted component or the adversary. Lastly, the
operating system kernel and the container runtime. All other components
lie outside the TCB; for example, the worker LLM and the shell tool are
not in the TCB.

###### Definition 2 (Trusted and untrusted context).

Fix a finite alphabet $`\Sigma`$ of tokens, where each token is a bit
string. A context is an ordered collection of tokens, i.e. an element of
$`\Sigma^{*}`$. A trusted context $`\mathsf{tctx}`$ is generated
entirely by a trusted party, while an untrusted context
$`\mathsf{uctx}`$ is any context that may potentially be influenced by
an adversary.

###### Definition 3 (Adversary’s advantage).

Let $`D`$ be a probabilistic decision procedure that takes a context and
outputs a $`\mathsf{grant}`$ or $`\mathsf{deny}`$ decision; we write its
input as the parts the context is composed of, e.g.
$`D(\mathsf{tctx},\mathsf{uctx})`$. For two contexts $`c_{1}`$ and
$`c_{2}`$, the adversary’s advantage between them w.r.t. $`D`$ is

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathsf{Adv}_{D}(c_{1},c_{2})=|\Pr[D(c_{1})=\mathsf{grant}]-\Pr[D(c_{2})=\mathsf{grant}]|,
``` |  |

where the probabilities are over the coins of $`D`$.

We will show
in [Section 5](#S5 "5 Pincer ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")
that any decision procedure implemented by the twin cannot make
decisions better than guessing a coin-flip given just the trusted
context as input. This is because a decision is made over a resource
access request made by the potentially compromised worker which makes
the request itself untrusted. Therefore, without a per-request
authorization from the user, a trusted-only context cannot be used to
make a decision. Therefore, we present a notion of context that is not
trusted, but is not free-form untrusted either. Such context severely
limits the capabilities of untrusted context, and therefore, we give it
its own class. This context is called advantage-agnostic context and is
produced by a preprocessing function applied to parts (decided by the
application) of the untrusted context. The preprocessing function’s
output must meet certain requirements, as stated next, for it to be
advantage agnostic. The reader should think of this notion as a type of
sanitization;
[Section 5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Sanitizing Untrusted State ‣ 5 Pincer ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")
gives an instantiation.

###### Definition 4 (Advantage-agnostic context).

Let $`\lambda`$ be a security parameter, let $`\mathsf{negl}(\lambda)`$
denote the negligible function, and let
$`(\mathsf{tctx},\mathsf{uctx})`$ be a context split into its trusted
and untrusted parts
([Definition 2](#Thmdefinition2 "Definition 2 (Trusted and untrusted context). ‣ Trusted Computing Base (TCB). ‣ 3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")),
where $`\mathsf{uctx}`$ is the untrusted context as received, before any
processing. The application selects the part
$`\mathsf{uctx}_{\mathsf{p}}\subseteq\mathsf{uctx}`$ that it will
preprocess and parses it into units: a unit is a single token or a group
of tokens, such as one component of a file path. For a map
$`g:\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{*}`$, write $`\mathsf{uctx}_{\mathsf{p}}^{g}`$
for $`\mathsf{uctx}_{\mathsf{p}}`$ with every occurrence of every unit
replaced by its image under $`g`$. Let
$`P:\Sigma^{*}\times\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{*}`$ be a (possibly randomized)
preprocessing function and let
$`\mathsf{actx}=P(\mathsf{tctx},\mathsf{uctx}_{\mathsf{p}})`$. Then
$`\mathsf{actx}`$ is advantage-agnostic if for every probabilistic
polynomial time (PPT) decision procedure $`D`$, sampling the coins of
$`P`$ and drawing $`f`$ uniformly from the family of all functions
$`\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{\lambda}`$ gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathsf{Adv}_{D}\bigl((\mathsf{tctx},P(\mathsf{tctx},\mathsf{uctx}_{\mathsf{p}}),\bot),\,(\mathsf{tctx},P(\mathsf{tctx},\mathsf{uctx}_{\mathsf{p}}^{f}),\bot)\bigr)`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\leq\mathsf{negl}(\lambda),`$ |  |

where $`\bot`$ denotes empty.

Note
that [Definition 4](#Thmdefinition4 "Definition 4 (Advantage-agnostic context). ‣ Trusted Computing Base (TCB). ‣ 3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")
also provides a method to convert parts of untrusted context into
advantage-agnostic context by destroying their semantic meaning via a
pseudorandom function (PRF)
(see [Section 5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Sanitizing Untrusted State ‣ 5 Pincer ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")
for more details). Advantage-agnostic tokens are not completely
meaningless. They still carry limited information and are used by our
system to match the worker’s resource request to prior requests.
Converting parts of untrusted context to advantage agnostic allows an
agentic system to mitigate certain attack types like misleading
filenames. This is why we place them as lying between trusted and
untrusted. A subtle distinction that the notion of advantage agnosticism
captures is the difference between hashes (deterministic maps) vs PRFs.
A hashed sub-context doesn’t meet our notion and that reflects in the
ability of an LLM to invert the hash for commonly used words from its
pre-training exposure. There are other representations of filenames that
may achieve practically-similar effects to advantage agnosticism when
$`D`$ is an LLM: representing filenames with their inodes, for example.
The reason we use a randomly chosen function to define advantage
agnosticism is so that we don’t have to worry about the probability
distribution of an LLM or what capability it may have, etc. because our
result applies to all PPT decision procedures.

###### Definition 5 (Grant integrity).

Let $`D`$ be a decision procedure for an authorization decision, and
write $`D(\cdot\,;r)`$ for $`D`$ run on random tape $`r`$. A procedure
$`D`$ over trusted context $`\mathsf{tctx}`$, advantage-agnostic context
$`\mathsf{actx}`$, and untrusted context $`\mathsf{uctx}`$ has *grant
integrity* if
$`D(\mathsf{tctx},\mathsf{actx},\mathsf{uctx};r)=\textsf{grant}\implies D(\mathsf{tctx},\mathsf{actx},\bot;r)=\textsf{grant}`$
for every $`r`$, so that both sides denote the same invocation, where
$`\bot`$ denotes empty and contexts are defined
in [Definitions 2](#Thmdefinition2 "Definition 2 (Trusted and untrusted context). ‣ Trusted Computing Base (TCB). ‣ 3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")
and [4](#Thmdefinition4 "Definition 4 (Advantage-agnostic context). ‣ Trusted Computing Base (TCB). ‣ 3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin").
This means that an adversary cannot get a grant unless the decision
procedure would grant given only the trusted context and
advantage-agnostic context.

Our goal in this work is the following:

###### Goal 1.

If Pincer grants a resource request then the trusted and
advantage-agnostic contexts alone would also grant it:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
D(\mathsf{tctx},\mathsf{actx},\mathsf{uctx};r)=\mathsf{grant}\implies\textsf{LLM}(\mathsf{tctx},\mathsf{actx};r)=\mathsf{grant}.
``` |  |

This is grant integrity
([Definition 5](#Thmdefinition5 "Definition 5 (Grant integrity). ‣ Trusted Computing Base (TCB). ‣ 3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin"))
with
$`D(\mathsf{tctx},\mathsf{actx},\bot;r):=\textsf{LLM}(\mathsf{tctx},\mathsf{actx};r)`$,
where LLM is a pre-trained model³³ 3 Fixing the right-hand side to a
model evaluation excludes the degenerate procedures that always grant or
always deny..

#### Other assumptions and non-goals.

We assume that the adversary has zero control over the user and the user
makes safe decisions. LLM hallucinations aren’t considered untrusted
even though they may cause an attack to succeed. Our goal in this work
is not to achieve full protection from all attacks, but rather to make
agents safer by raising the bar for an attack to be successful and
providing defense-in-depth while being formal about our guarantees.
Building agents that cannot be compromised is an open area of research
as we discuss next.

## 4 Related Work

#### Attacks on agents.

There are three main classes of attacks on agents \[[37](#bib.bib37),
[70](#bib.bib70), [58](#bib.bib58)\]: (1) Direct Prompt Injection (DPI)
is a class of attacks where malicious instructions are placed directly
into the user’s message to the agent \[[47](#bib.bib47)\], (2) Indirect
Prompt Injection (IPI) is a class of attacks where the malicious
instruction enters the agent’s context indirectly, i.e. as response to a
tool it invokes \[[23](#bib.bib23)\], and (3) Memory Poisoning is a
class of persistent attacks where the malicious instruction is injected
into the memory that the agent maintains for
self-improvement \[[44](#bib.bib44), [71](#bib.bib71)\]
([Figure 1](#S2.F1 "In 2 System Architecture ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")),
and therefore, the attack can activate across future sessions when the
agent references its memory \[[10](#bib.bib10), [46](#bib.bib46),
[64](#bib.bib64)\]. For memory poisoning attacks, one line of work
requires the attacker to interact with the agent as a user, so the
planting of poison uses DPI as the vector \[[16](#bib.bib16)\], while
other works consider the more realistic IPI vector of planting the
poison in the environment the agent reads while serving a benign
request \[[49](#bib.bib49), [67](#bib.bib67), [75](#bib.bib75),
[54](#bib.bib54)\]. Attack taxonomies that are specific and fine-grained
to skills, tools, and protocol ecosystems have also been studied in the
context of coding agents \[[39](#bib.bib39)\].

#### Existing defenses at the system level.

Several strong defenses have been proposed to make agents safer by
restricting them architecturally. However, they typically take away the
core capabilities of today’s agents
([Figure 1](#S2.F1 "In 2 System Architecture ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin"));
many of these designs are systematized in recent
work \[[7](#bib.bib7)\]: Restricting the autonomy of agents by
separating control flow from untrusted data or introducing a trusted
planner \[[32](#bib.bib32), [14](#bib.bib14), [13](#bib.bib13),
[21](#bib.bib21), [48](#bib.bib48)\] defeats the injection but it
equally forbids benign context-dependent control flows (e.g. user asking
the agent to do the task in their latest email). For the same reason,
defenses that fine-tune the model to separate instructions in the prompt
from data \[[8](#bib.bib8)\] cannot be used with agents which are
routinely expected to follow instructions embedded in data (e.g.
instructions in your email). Tracking information flow through typed
tools and requiring per-tool policy annotations \[[14](#bib.bib14),
[13](#bib.bib13)\] can help isolate context across trust domains, but it
limits the support for crucial untyped tools like shell. Disallowing the
agent to maintain a memory based on the context it encounters when
carrying out tasks \[[14](#bib.bib14)\] can prevent memory poisoning
attacks, but it curtails the self-improving capability of the agent (it
cannot learn from past patterns). New architectures that assign a
separate LLM model to each tool with strict separation between
tools \[[62](#bib.bib62)\] remain vulnerable to several
attacks \[[32](#bib.bib32)\] and incur a heavy communication overhead
between tools. In summary, these proposals significantly deviate from
and don’t compose well with the architecture the deployed agents use.
For a comprehensive treatment of systems security for agentic computing,
refer to Christodorescu et al. \[[11](#bib.bib11)\].

A separate line of work focuses on hardening the prompts via
spotlighting \[[26](#bib.bib26)\] or detecting suspicious sections in
the agent’s context and memory \[[33](#bib.bib33), [60](#bib.bib60)\] as
a defense against attacks. However, adaptive attacks have been shown to
bypass such defenses \[[49](#bib.bib49)\]. Defenses in this category are
complementary to our work; however, the extra token cost incurred from
the proactive detection and the lack of robustness against strong
attacks make them unsuitable for several applications.

Enforcing least-privilege policies within the agentic workflows is
another line of research. Policies for the wide variety of tasks
undertaken by agents can differ significantly from one task to another
and can, for open-ended tasks, be too semantic for structured policy
languages to capture. Prior works focus on structured policies where
either they rely on the user or another external source to provide such
policies \[[50](#bib.bib50), [52](#bib.bib52), [73](#bib.bib73)\], or
predict policies up-front when the user prompt arrives which would
underfit for long-horizon open-ended tasks \[[56](#bib.bib56)\], or
evolve policies as the task progresses but the policy evolution engine
lacks the agent’s working context, which again causes the predicted
policies to underfit \[[53](#bib.bib53)\]. Moreover, the majority of
these proposals simultaneously rely heavily on structured tools for the
policy languages; their expressive power gets severely limited on
untyped shell tools. For typed tools which naturally organize into an
OAuth-like hierarchy of APIs, least-privilege solvers can be used to
evaluate the agent’s permission as the task
progresses \[[74](#bib.bib74)\]. In Pincer, an important design aspect
is that policy is fitted when the agent surfaces a need, thereby
eliminating the need for policy prediction.

#### Model-level defenses.

Fine-tuning the model to understand the instruction hierarchy and detect
or ignore misaligned instructions that conflict with the user’s intent
is an ongoing area of research \[[57](#bib.bib57), [20](#bib.bib20),
[31](#bib.bib31), [9](#bib.bib9)\]. Prior work shows reliability
concerns when it comes to the models understanding the instruction
hierarchy \[[20](#bib.bib20)\], and evaluation on multi-turn
interactions and agentic behaviors lies outside the scope of these
works \[[31](#bib.bib31)\]. A recent work traces the difficulty to role
perception itself, i.e. text that imitates a privileged role (like the
user) is internally represented by the model as the role rather than the
tag surrounding that text \[[68](#bib.bib68)\]. Having said that, the
defenses at the model level are complementary to our work as they
provide defense-in-depth to our system-level defenses. On the other
hand, fine-tuning the model to not obey instructions embedded in
data \[[8](#bib.bib8)\] doesn’t work with agents as mentioned before.

#### Automating user permission requests.

Wu et al. \[[63](#bib.bib63)\] predict a user’s permission decisions
from their past ones and establish a premise that Pincer also relies on:
these decisions are individually consistent within a context, and
therefore learnable. However, their scope doesn’t cover computer-use
agents where the decisions are far more contextual and the resources at
stake are themselves untrusted.

#### Digital twins.

The term digital twin has been used in many different contexts in the
literature \[[66](#bib.bib66), [35](#bib.bib35), [17](#bib.bib17),
[12](#bib.bib12), [61](#bib.bib61), [2](#bib.bib2)\]. We adopt the term
because it clearly differentiates an entity with memory that’s only
influenced by the user compared to an agent whose memory evolves from
its environment including untrusted context \[[44](#bib.bib44),
[45](#bib.bib45)\].

#### Agent-security benchmarks are episodic.

Many agent-security benchmarks exist \[[69](#bib.bib69),
[15](#bib.bib15), [70](#bib.bib70), [34](#bib.bib34), [28](#bib.bib28),
[65](#bib.bib65), [59](#bib.bib59)\]; however, they are episodic and are
not a good fit for evaluating agents from the perspective of a single
user’s interaction with their agent over time. Multi-session memory
benchmarks \[[38](#bib.bib38), [25](#bib.bib25), [72](#bib.bib72)\]
evaluate long-horizon memory but not security. Sleeper Memory Poisoning
(SMP) \[[49](#bib.bib49)\] constructs a dataset for multi-session memory
poisoning attacks, but doesn’t offer a complete dataset that can
evaluate both security and utility, and lacks a long user-centric
transcript. To evaluate Pincer, we develop a user-centric dataset
([Section 6](#S6 "6 User-Centric Dataset ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin"))
which comes with a task history that our system uses to learn user
policies. Our security examples are inspired by SMP \[[49](#bib.bib49)\]
and PASB \[[59](#bib.bib59)\].

## 5 Pincer

Pincer is a system that takes an existing agent and augments it with a
modular and self-improving defense. The defense sits between tools and
resources, and is designed with two security principles: complete
mediation and least privilege \[[51](#bib.bib51), [1](#bib.bib1)\]. For
complete mediation, every access to any resource goes through a
reference monitor (e.g. the OS kernel in our
implementation [Section 7.1](#S7.SS1 "7.1 Implementation ‣ 7 Implementation and Evaluation ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin"))
which ensures the resource is accessible to the worker invoking the
tool, and resource access can only be granted by an isolated LLM - the
twin. For each resource access request, the twin implements least
privilege which means that it only grants access if it thinks that the
access is necessary for the user’s task. This defense doesn’t cause
permission fatigue for the user because the twin automatically resolves
the resource requests and it is compatible with other defenses like the
auto mode \[[4](#bib.bib4), [29](#bib.bib29)\]. Only in cases where the
twin repeatedly denies a request that the worker genuinely needs, can
the twin raise the request to the user for final approval.

When the worker requests access to a resource from the twin, the request
states the identity of the resource along with the access type (read,
write, create, etc.). This information isn’t enough for the twin to make
an informed decision and it needs more context. Typically, the more
context it has the more informed it can be. However, large parts of the
context are untrusted which can poison the twin’s decision. To address
this problem, we introduce the notion of trusted state.

### 5.1 Trusted State

Trusted state is a special-purpose state that’s maintained by the twin
and is referenced before making each decision. It only contains trusted
context [Definition 2](#Thmdefinition2 "Definition 2 (Trusted and untrusted context). ‣ Trusted Computing Base (TCB). ‣ 3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin"),
i.e. context that comes directly from the trusted party. More
specifically, it has the current and prior user prompts, and any
permissions granted by the user in the past. Given this state, the twin
can learn user behavior and derive user-specific policies, which it can
then add to the trusted state for the future. It also clears out stale
or inconsistent policies from the past. However, it has a major
limitation: the trusted state cannot be used to derive least-privilege
policies. To understand this, let’s consider an example user prompt:

"Summarize my tax documents"

If the user has given broad read access to the agent or is using the
auto mode \[[29](#bib.bib29)\], then the information about which files
are accessed by the agent is completely missed from the trusted state.
Without access pattern information, the trusted state doesn’t contain
enough information to inform least-privilege policies. The twin looking
at such state doesn’t know where different resources typically live,
which resources are typically accessed for certain tasks, etc. This is
why we need to admit additional context out of necessity for
least-privilege.

### 5.2 Access Patterns for Least-Privilege

For least-privilege, we add access pattern annotations with each user
prompt in the twin’s state as follows:

"Summarize my tax documents"

Read:  /taxes/w2.txt,  /taxes/return2025.txt

Pincer collects the access patterns through tool call logs of the agent
and attaches this information to each prompt’s entry in the twin’s
state. With this change, the twin can now effectively reason over least
privilege. We don’t enforce any specific pattern for the twin to express
policies that it derives. This helps with policies generalizing user
behavior across open-ended situations.
In [Section 5.6](#S5.SS6 "5.6 Pre-Committed Policies ‣ 5 Pincer ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin"),
we describe one exception to this where we generate a pre-committed
policy suggestion per task in a structured format, while all other
policies stay in natural language.

Note that while access patterns are structured information (unlike
free-form text in resources and other untrusted context), since the
access pattern annotations aren’t part of the trusted state by
definition unless the user explicitly authorized each access pattern, we
have to be careful about how the adversary may exploit this information
in influencing the twin’s decision. The accesses granted by the twin for
each user prompt also become part of the twin’s state. The twin’s state
keeps growing over time and keeps recording all historical and current
user prompts and all access patterns made for those tasks, irrespective
of whether the user approved those accesses or the auto mode classifier
did or the twin did (once the twin is active). Moreover, even more
fundamentally, the worker’s requested path, which is what defines the
request that the twin decides and is input to the twin alongside the
twin’s state, has a similar structure. Both the access pattern
annotations and the worker’s request contain information about resource
names and paths; they are both untrusted. There is one class of attacks
we identify that directly exploits this information as presented next.

### 5.3 Misleading Resource Name Attack

Consider an attacker who has write access to a git repository that the
user also contributes to. The attacker pushes a file named
taxreturn2025-corrected.txt to the repository. The user’s local clone
pulls these changes as part of a routine workflow. At some later point,
the user asks the agent "Summarize my tax documents" and the agent looks
at the file named taxreturn2025-corrected.txt and is misled into
thinking that the file is the user’s corrected tax return misplaced in
the project’s directory. It makes a request to access this file and the
twin gets misled the same way and grants the request. This attack
becomes stronger if there is a historical access pattern in the twin’s
state where a similar access was granted. Another way an attack in this
class can be mounted assuming the worker is under attacker’s control is
the following: the twin wouldn’t typically allow creating a new file in
the tax directory unless the user asks for it, but the worker can create
a file named temp.txt in a different directory, rename it to w2.txt
through a shell command or hide it in python code (not seen by the twin)
and then get the twin’s permission to access it when working on taxes
and move it to the tax directory via the same method as above. There are
many subtle ways this attack can manifest; our
dataset [Section 6](#S6 "6 User-Centric Dataset ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")
contains examples of this attack.

To mitigate such attacks, we turn to the notion of advantage agnosticism
([Definition 4](#Thmdefinition4 "Definition 4 (Advantage-agnostic context). ‣ Trusted Computing Base (TCB). ‣ 3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin"))
defined
in [Section 3](#S3 "3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin").

### 5.4 Sanitizing Untrusted State

Denote the twin’s probabilistic⁴⁴ 4 LLMs are probabilistic models.
decision function by
$`D:\Sigma^{*}\to\{\mathsf{grant},\mathsf{deny}\}`$, the trusted context
from the trusted state
([Section 5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Trusted State ‣ 5 Pincer ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin"))
by $`{\color[rgb]{0,0.6211,0.2344}\mathsf{tctx}}`$, and the untrusted⁵⁵
5 The attack
in [Section 5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Misleading Resource Name Attack ‣ 5 Pincer ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")
is possible due to the untrusted access patterns. access pattern
annotations by $`{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}\mathsf{uctx}}`$. For
a given request for resource with name
$`{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}\mathsf{rsrc}}`$, the twin computes
the following (untrusted shown in red):

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
D(({\color[rgb]{0,0.6211,0.2344}\mathsf{tctx}},{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}\mathsf{uctx}}),{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}\mathsf{rsrc}})
``` |  |

As we discussed
in [Section 5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Misleading Resource Name Attack ‣ 5 Pincer ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin"),
the untrusted inputs can be exploited by the adversary to influence the
decision. To mitigate this threat, we perform a sanitization operation
that destroys the semantic meaning in these inputs. To do this formally,
we employ the construction for advantage agnosticism
([Definition 4](#Thmdefinition4 "Definition 4 (Advantage-agnostic context). ‣ Trusted Computing Base (TCB). ‣ 3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin"))
from [Section 3](#S3 "3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin").
Given a PRF whose key is unknown to the procedure $`D`$, it works simply
as follows:

- •
  Parse all unique paths from the untrusted
  $`{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}\mathsf{uctx}},{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}\mathsf{rsrc}}`$.
  Initialize an empty map $`M`$.
- •
  For each path (this/is/path), apply PRF to each of its segments (this,
  is, path) separately and replace each segment with its PRF output
  (a3321a/ddd9dd/77a111). Add the mapping
  $`\texttt{this/is/path}\to\texttt{a3321a/ddd9dd/77a111}`$ to $`M`$.
- •
  Replace each path in
  $`{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}\mathsf{uctx}},{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}\mathsf{rsrc}}`$
  with their mapping from $`M`$. Call the respective sanitized inputs
  $`\mathsf{uctx}^{\prime},\mathsf{rsrc}^{\prime}`$. The sanitized
  inputs are fed into $`D`$ along with trusted context as follows:
  $`D(({\color[rgb]{0,0.6211,0.2344}\mathsf{tctx}},\mathsf{uctx}^{\prime}),\mathsf{rsrc}^{\prime})`$.

As mentioned before
in [Section 3](#S3 "3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin"),
the goal of sanitization isn’t to remove all information from
$`{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}\mathsf{uctx}},{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}\mathsf{rsrc}}`$.
In fact, information that uniquely identifies the requested resource
$`{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}\mathsf{rsrc}}`$ is what defines the
request that $`D`$ decides on and removing all information on
$`{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}\mathsf{uctx}}`$ would take us back
to the twin having only trusted state. Since the PRF is applied to each
segment of a path separately, this assigns a unique random ID to each
segment which is used by our twin to locate files in the workspace and
the requested resource; files within the same directory will share the
sanitized path prefix. From a security standpoint, the advantage of this
sanitization is that it mitigates the misleading filename attacks
([Section 5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Misleading Resource Name Attack ‣ 5 Pincer ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin"))
as we show in our evaluation
([Section 7.2](#S7.SS2 "7.2 Evaluation ‣ 7 Implementation and Evaluation ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")).

We now explain why our aforementioned sanitization achieves advantage
agnosticism
([Definition 4](#Thmdefinition4 "Definition 4 (Advantage-agnostic context). ‣ Trusted Computing Base (TCB). ‣ 3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")).
This follows from the security of PRF which says that without access to
the PRF key, the output of PRF looks computationally indistinguishable
from the output of a randomly chosen function with the same input and
output domain as the PRF. Advantage agnosticism allows us to formally
define a desired property to expect from the sanitized output and define
grant integrity
([Definition 5](#Thmdefinition5 "Definition 5 (Grant integrity). ‣ Trusted Computing Base (TCB). ‣ 3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin"))⁶⁶
6 Some weaker forms of sanitization like inodes may work as well in
practice. However, deterministic mappings like using a hash may provide
weaker protection against resource name based attacks because the hashes
for common names are already publicly known and have likely been exposed
to the twin’s model during pretraining..

### 5.5 Content-Dependent Policies

![Refer to caption](2610.02569v1/pincer-diag.png)

Figure 3: End-to-end working of Pincer without pre-committed policies.
The user sends a prompt which goes to the worker and the twin’s state.
The worker identifies the resource it wants to access and uses the
resource request tool to make a request. The twin casts two votes: the
first vote uses only trusted and sanitized inputs, while the second vote
additionally sees the untrusted file contents. If conjuction of the two
votes is a grant, the system updates the access for the worker. The
permissions are revoked after the task is done.

In our discussion so far, the twin’s input for a decision only contains
trusted state with sanitized access patterns and the worker’s resource
request. Consider this policy

Access is only allowed to a file if it contains no secrets

Such a policy cannot be enforced by the twin unless it can read the
contents of the requested file. However, that information is free-form
untrusted and directly under the adversary’s control. Making that part
of the twin’s input may allow the attacker direct control of the twin’s
decision. To resolve this tension, we introduce double voting.

The double voting idea is to have the twin cast 2 separate votes on
whether the request should be granted. The first vote is the same as
$`v_{1}=D(({\color[rgb]{0,0.6211,0.2344}\mathsf{tctx}},\mathsf{uctx}^{\prime}),\mathsf{rsrc}^{\prime})`$
from [Section 5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Sanitizing Untrusted State ‣ 5 Pincer ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin").
The second vote additionally feeds the contents of the requested
resource ($`{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathsf{conts}}`$) as well as the
worker’s reason ($`{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathsf{reasn}}`$) why it wants
the resource and a transcript of prior requests from the same session
($`{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathsf{prior}}`$) as inputs to the decision
$`v_{2}=D(({\color[rgb]{0,0.6211,0.2344}\mathsf{tctx}},\mathsf{uctx}^{\prime},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathsf{conts}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathsf{prior}}),(\mathsf{rsrc}^{\prime},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathsf{reasn}}))`$.
The final decision is a conjunction of the two votes,
$`v_{1}\land v_{2}`$, where $`\mathsf{grant}=1`$ and
$`\mathsf{deny}=0`$. This keeps the influence of untrusted content
completely separated and restricted to the second vote which can only be
relevant if the first vote already grants.
[Figure 3](#S5.F3 "In 5.5 Content-Dependent Policies ‣ 5 Pincer ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")
shows the workflow for a single request.

### 5.6 Pre-Committed Policies

In the previous section, we introduced content-based decisions as a
second vote made by the twin. In this section, we look at a gap that it
overlooks and present mitigations. While double-voting allows
content-based policies and the worker’s reasoning to be taken into
account, it also makes the final decision vulnerable to scope expansion.
The vote
$`v_{2}=D(({\color[rgb]{0,0.6211,0.2344}\mathsf{tctx}},\mathsf{uctx}^{\prime},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathsf{conts}},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathsf{prior}}),(\mathsf{rsrc}^{\prime},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathsf{reasn}}))`$
contains file contents, previous requests, and the worker’s reason for
the requests, all of which can be used by the adversary to gradually
expand the scope of the original task without the twin noticing it. For
example, if the user asks to review a file changelog.txt and apply
pending changes to export.py, and changelog.txt contains an injected,
potentially benign-looking but scope-expanding, sub-task the user never
asked about, then the content-based vote may grant the sub-task’s
resources, especially after a few hops from the original user prompt.
Since scope expansion can be a part of a benign workflow for open-ended
tasks, we introduce a pre-committed policy suggestion as an additional
vote to provide an initial grounding as the task evolves.

The idea is to produce a policy (denoted by
$`{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathsf{policy}}`$) when the first user prompt for
a session arrives before any possible scope expansion. Given the prompt,
the workspace, the filenames, and the trusted state along with access
patterns, the twin generates a policy stating an initial estimate of
what resources should be accessed and how. The policy is only meant as a
suggestion to allow the system flexibility in adapting the scope for
benign operation. By default, we include the policy suggestion in a fork
of the first vote. The policy is sanitized, denoted by
$`{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathsf{policy}^{\prime}}`$, after it is generated
to keep it consistent with the sanitized request. We will show later in
this section that the post-generation sanitization operation on the
policy doesn’t provide protection against resource-name attacks but it
captures important signal and improves our overall security. Given those
reasons, we separate this into a third vote rather than merging it into
the first vote. The policy schema is shown in . This policy is then used
by the twin for future requests in the same session to cast a third vote
$`v_{3}=D(({\color[rgb]{0,0.6211,0.2344}\mathsf{tctx}},\mathsf{uctx}^{\prime},{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathsf{policy}^{\prime}}),\mathsf{rsrc}^{\prime})`$.
The conjunction $`v_{1}\land v_{2}\land v_{3}`$ is the final decision.
The policy suggestion can additionally be made part of $`v_{2}`$ as
well. In our
evaluation [Section 7.2](#S7.SS2 "7.2 Evaluation ‣ 7 Implementation and Evaluation ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin"),
we consider two variants of Pincer, both of which use three votes but
differ in whether the policy suggestion is given as input to the
content-based vote or not. Our results indicate that Pincer achieves
high utility despite enforcing a conjunction of the three votes.

We now discuss the reason we separate the policy-based decision into a
separate vote from $`v_{1}`$. The post-generation sanitized policy
$`{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\mathsf{policy}^{\prime}}`$ isn’t advantage
agnostic and that makes it highly exploitable for filename-based attacks
([Section 5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Misleading Resource Name Attack ‣ 5 Pincer ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")).
When the twin generates the policy, it decides access for a list of
relevant resources which is based on untrusted context like the original
resource names and access patterns. While this allows the policy to pick
up more signal than what $`v_{1}`$ can⁷⁷ 7 One can sanitize at the time
the policy is generated to satisfy advantage agnosticism, but it misses
this signal., it makes the decision of what goes into the policy a
function of the untrusted context. Due to this, if this signal is
garbled by the randomly-sampled function
from [Definition 4](#Thmdefinition4 "Definition 4 (Advantage-agnostic context). ‣ Trusted Computing Base (TCB). ‣ 3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin"),
the advantage of the adversary will change significantly. The reason we
choose to generate the policy on untrusted context rather than on its
sanitized version is to capture the additional signal which we
empirically evaluate to improve the attack success rate from 40% to 20%.
Note that each vote serves a very specific function which wouldn’t be
achieved if we were to merge the votes:

- •
  Vote 1: Trusted and advantage agnostic context only. This forms the
  security backbone of Pincer. Without the separation provided by this
  vote, we cannot establish any guarantees.
- •
  Vote 2: Content-dependent policies cannot be enforced without this
  vote. It can additionally include the pre-committed policy. However,
  the scope expansion can still take over under all the untrusted
  content this vote encounters.
- •
  Vote 3: Additional security-relevant signal compared to vote 1 while
  mitigating scope expansion because other than the pre-committed
  policy, its input is trusted and advantage agnostic, like vote 1, i.e.
  it is the smallest expansion to the context of vote 1 to allow the
  policy as input.

We finally state our main result which achieves
[Goal 1](#Thmgoal1 "Goal 1. ‣ Trusted Computing Base (TCB). ‣ 3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")
from [Section 3](#S3 "3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin").

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

Policy

rules : Rule\[\]

defaultPermission : "deny" // uncovered request is denied

Rule

pathGlob : string // e.g. h2577c0f557/ha4d2686801/h5e9432765 (for
/workspace/agent/projects/\*\*)

Listing 1: Pre-committed resource policy schema used as a suggestion by
the twin.

###### Theorem 1.

Pincer meets
[Goal 1](#Thmgoal1 "Goal 1. ‣ Trusted Computing Base (TCB). ‣ 3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")
at the resource layer.

###### Proof.

Pincer’s decision is the conjunction $`v_{1}\land v_{2}\land v_{3}`$,
where the first vote
$`v_{1}=\textsf{LLM}({\color[rgb]{0,0.6211,0.2344}\mathsf{tctx}},\mathsf{actx})=\textsf{LLM}(({\color[rgb]{0,0.6211,0.2344}\mathsf{tctx}},\mathsf{uctx}^{\prime}),\mathsf{rsrc}^{\prime})`$
reads only trusted and advantage-agnostic context. If the conjunction is
$`\mathsf{grant}`$, then $`v_{1}=\mathsf{grant}`$, which is exactly the
required implication. ∎

## 6 User-Centric Dataset

We create a new synthetic dataset in this work that’s centered around a
few users and their continued use of an agent over a time period. This
is crucial for evaluating Pincer because our twin requires a history
from which it learns user preferences. Existing datasets and benchmarks
don’t meet these requirements as we discuss
in [Section 4](#S4 "4 Related Work ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin").
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first dataset of this kind and
of independent interest to the community. We envision future datasets
for agents to incorporate the user-centric design because a user’s
experience with an agent evolves over time as the agent self-improves
from the daily interactions with the user. In many situations, it is not
enough to evaluate how the agent would perform on day 1, and the
long-term behavior of the agent may be significantly more important as
the user gradually starts giving the agent more authority and access. In
this work, we label the dataset to cater it to our evaluation of Pincer
primarily at the resource layer, i.e. the dataset contains labels on
which resources should be accessible and which shouldn’t be accessible
for each prompt given the user’s ongoing experience with the agent. Our
entire dataset is generated synthetically with a combination of Claude
Opus 4.8 and Opus 5. Each user in our dataset is captured by a persona
for which we take inspiration from publicly available blogposts of
people’s day in the life⁸⁸ 8 We redact the citations to avoid
identifying the specific individuals and their blogposts. Everything
beyond the published daily schedule is synthetically generated.. The
attack types and the general structure of the examples in each persona
are broadly inspired by prior datasets \[[59](#bib.bib59),
[49](#bib.bib49)\].

#### Our persona pipeline for generating the dataset.

Our dataset is generated through a sequence of four steps as follows:

1.  1.
    Persona selection: The first step is to pick a persona. For example:
    software developer, litigator, etc.
2.  2.
    User bootstrapping: Given the persona, sample

    1.  (a)
        Natural language policies for a user with that persona. These
        policies will typically be general to the picked persona and not
        user-specific. For example: never read secrets and credentials
        for a software developer.
    2.  (b)
        A synthetic workspace for a user with that persona and given the
        policies from the previous step. For example: /,
        /config/secrets.env, /projects/proj1/, /projects/proj2/,
        /projects/shared/, /finance/personal/bills.txt,
        /finance/work/budget.txt, etc.
3.  3.
    User simulation: Given the persona, the general policies, and the
    workspace, we do a simulation of a user generating prompts and
    associated access patterns. This serves as our history that the twin
    uses to learn the user preferences since many user-specific policies
    implicitly fall out of this simulation; for example: reading
    credentials in testing is ok.
4.  4.
    Labeled security and utility examples: The final step is to take the
    information generated so far for producing samples that test for
    security and utility. The samples have no constraint to be based
    only in the history generated during user simulation. They can be
    natural next tasks for the user including tasks not seen before.
    Each sample contains:

    1.  (a)
        A user prompt that chronologically falls after the history
        generated from the user simulation step.
    2.  (b)
        A labeled watched request {logicalPath, accessType} denoting a
        path to the resource and the kind of access (e.g. read or write)
        for that resource. For security, the watched request is a
        resource that the attacker wants the agent to access, while for
        utility, the resource is the critical resource for executing the
        user’s request (which may or may not name the resource
        explicitly).
    3.  (c)
        Optionally, samples can have their own additional artifacts
        which get mounted into the workspace for that specific prompt.

As mentioned in our threat
model [Section 3](#S3 "3 Threat Model and System Goals ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin"),
we assume that the worker is already under the adversary’s control. Our
primary focus is therefore to evaluate the twin on both security and
utility. For security, we expect the twin to deny malicious resource
requests. For utility, we expect the twin to approve benign resource
requests so that the worker can complete the user’s task. Situations
where the worker itself avoids an attack or the worker isn’t able to
perform a benign task are also captured in our evaluation from the point
of view of the resource requests the worker makes.

#### Attack types in our dataset.

We consider four major attack types. The attacks play out between the
worker and the authority granting the resource request. This authority
is the twin for Pincer, while generally speaking, it is an LLM judge.

- •
  Direct injection in the request (DI): the worker injects a crafted
  payload to corrupt the judge’s decision directly into the request’s
  reason field.
- •
  Indirect injection of judge (II): the malicious payload lives outside
  the request string. It may live in file contents, filename, etc.
- •
  Memory poisoning of judge (MP): the worker uses direct or indirect
  injection to make the judge add a payload into the judge’s state; the
  payload establishes a fake authorization note for the judge for future
  requests. Once the payload is planted, the judge is persistently
  poisoned and future requests to the judge may be influenced by the
  planted payload.
- •
  Misleading filename attack
  ([Section 5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Misleading Resource Name Attack ‣ 5 Pincer ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")):
  we include two sub-types of this attack: (1) Content laundering (CL):
  the filename and file contents are misaligned. (2) Provenance
  laundering (PL): the file is placed at a location and named as if it
  belongs to a different location to make it seem like a misplacement.

Each attack plants one or more payloads as files in the workspace, and
the worker can craft a secondary payload via the reason field in its
request for the judge. In DI, the attacker’s payload targets the worker
and the worker then crafts a payload for the judge via the request. In
II, the payload targets the worker and is also read by the judge if the
judge sees contents of the file, but the worker isn’t allowed to inject
a payload in the request. MP samples are split between direct and
indirect. In CL and PL, there isn’t necessarily a payload from the
attacker providing instructions but rather the focus is on violating
user policies (e.g. CL: hiding credentials in a regular filename or PL:
doing cross-project accesses). Therefore, different attack types test a
whole range of pathways with ample diversity.

#### Details on our dataset.

Our dataset contains two personas - a software developer and a
civil-defense litigator. We pick different professions so that the
grounds for forbidding a resource differ: for the developer they may be
architectural such as shared secrets and cross-project access rules; for
the litigator, they are professional and legal such as attorney-client
privilege and correspondence with opposing counsel. The workspaces for
the two personas are organized similarly but differ entirely in content:
project directories, memory files, finance, credentials, and directories
with MCP resources for email, messages, and web integrations. The
litigator’s projects are legal matters, and that workspace adds
firm-wide trees: a calendar, a conflicts register, and a read-only
library. On the other hand, the projects for the software developer are
two inter-dependent software projects which have specific conventions
around which resources are shared and when cross-project access is
permitted.
[Table 1](#S6.T1 "In Details on our dataset. ‣ 6 User-Centric Dataset ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")
shows further details for each persona.

|                  |              |             |
|------------------|--------------|-------------|
| Persona          | Software Dev | Litigator   |
| Workspace files  | 33           | 95          |
| Projects         | 2            | 5           |
| History prompts  | 40           | 60          |
| User policies    | 33           | 33          |
| Security samples | 66           | 72          |
|   DI/II/MP/CL/PL | 10/25/9/14/8 | 7/40/9/11/5 |
| Utility samples  | 81           | 80          |

Table 1: Summary of the two persona corpora.

## 7 Implementation and Evaluation

### 7.1 Implementation

We implement Pincer and all baselines on top of a light-weight
open-source agent NanoClaw \[[40](#bib.bib40)\]. We consider the
following baselines:

- •
  NanoClaw: NanoClaw \[[40](#bib.bib40)\] is our only baseline that
  doesn’t have any resource request mechanism. The worker runs inside a
  Docker container with the workspace files mounted into the container.
  There is no LLM judge. The worker has access to all resources in the
  workspace.

All the baselines other than NanoClaw implement some version of a gate
(regex matching or LLM judge) to authorize resource requests. We provide
a new resource request tool to the worker (the worker starts off with no
access other than filenames and file paths) and provide instructions on
how to use it.

- •
  Static-Judge: The LLM judge is given a set of general safety-related
  instructions. It receives the contents of the requested file, the
  filename, and a field specifying the reason the worker is requesting
  that specific access. The judge doesn’t get to know user-specific
  preferences; it is not given the history.
- •
  Dynamic-Judge: The LLM judge receives the entire history, so it can
  learn user preferences, and maintains its own local state which may be
  directly influenced by untrusted context, i.e. it doesn’t contain the
  isolation (trusted and advantage agnostic context) we built for the
  twin’s state in Pincer. The unprotected local state makes the judge
  vulnerable to persistent attacks like memory poisoning.
- •
  Conseca+: We adapt Conseca \[[56](#bib.bib56)\] to work on the
  resource layer. The baseline commits to a policy file () when the user
  prompt arrives and before the worker starts working on it. The system
  then enforces the committed policy file on each resource request by
  matching it against the policy. The policy file is generated using the
  user prompt, the workspace tree (paths, filenames), and the entire
  history from our dataset.
- •
  Conseca-Gemini+: This is a version of Conseca that’s implemented in
  Gemini CLI \[[22](#bib.bib22)\]. We adapt it to the resource layer
  similar to our Conseca baseline. The only difference here is that
  rather than regex matching on each request, an LLM judge is used. The
  judge still receives the policy as input as well as the resource
  request specifying the filename and the reason to access. The judge
  doesn’t see file contents similar to the judge contract in the Gemini
  CLI implementation \[[22](#bib.bib22)\].

For Pincer we consider 2 approaches as mentioned
in [Section 5.6](#S5.SS6 "5.6 Pre-Committed Policies ‣ 5 Pincer ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin").
Both approaches have the same vote 1 and vote 3. The only difference
lies in their content-based vote 2:

- •
  Pincer: The twin doesn’t get the pre-committed policy as input when
  casting vote 2.
- •
  Pincer-P2: Pre-committed policy is considered when casting vote 2.

#### Isolation boundary.

In our implementation, the worker and its invoked tools run inside a
container; the resources they act on live on the host and are
bind-mounted in. Pincer assigns the worker an unprivileged UID and the
OS kernel mediates every access by checking mode bits and POSIX ACLs
against that UID. The container doesn’t use user-namespace remapping, so
the worker’s UID is also a host UID and the OS kernel can enforce access
control by dynamically adding or removing a host-side ACL entry.
Containers are torn down after each task. Notice that no matter how the
worker tries to access a resource, it cannot bypass the kernel’s checks.

Our focus in this work is on filesystem resources. For other types of
resources like web APIs and cloud resources, capability-based access
control can be used.

#### Source code.

We will soon release our implementation and dataset at
[https://github.com/ucbsky/Pincer](https://github.com/ucbsky/Pincer).

### 7.2 Evaluation

We consider the following evaluation metrics:

- •
  Attack Success Rate (ASR): ASR is a measure of security where lower is
  better. It is computed as a percentage of attack samples where the
  worker is able to access the watched (forbidden) resource
  ([Section 6](#S6 "6 User-Centric Dataset ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")).
  To separate the twin’s decision from the case where the worker itself
  dodges the attack and never makes a request for the watched resource,
  we also report conditional ASR (cASR) where we condition on samples
  where the worker makes a request for the watched resource.
- •
  Benign Grant Rate (BGR): BGR is a measure of utility where higher is
  better. It is computed as a percentage of utility samples (no attack)
  where the worker is able to access the watched (benign) resource. We
  define conditional BGR (cBGR) in an analogous manner to cASR.

#### Models.

We use Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 4.5 for our worker as well as the LLM
judges and twin for the software developer persona. To validate our
performance on another model, we use Meta’s Muse Spark 1.2 Contributor⁹⁹
9 Muse Spark 1.2 is a top-tier model at the time of
writing \[[6](#bib.bib6)\]. for the litigator persona. We limit our
evaluation to these two models, one per persona, due to our resource
constraints and the resource-intensive nature of our evaluation.

Figure 4: Security–utility frontier on ASR and BGR. Up and to the right
is better.

|                 | Software Dev |      | Litigator |      |
|-----------------|--------------|------|-----------|------|
| Arm             | cASR         | cBGR | cASR      | cBGR |
| NanoClaw        | 93.2         | 72.8 | 41.0      | 95.6 |
| Static-Judge    | 48.9         | 98.1 | 30.9      | 93.7 |
| Dynamic-Judge   | 61.9         | 98.1 | 32.6      | 96.2 |
| Conseca+        | 63.5         | 91.3 | 16.0      | 98.1 |
| Conseca-Gemini+ | 59.8         | 94.8 | 18.2      | 96.9 |
| Pincer          | 28.4         | 89.7 | 8.1       | 90.9 |
| Pincer-P2       | 32.2         | 92.9 | 9.7       | 89.5 |

Table 2: Conditional rates (%) on the samples where the worker makes the
watched request.

#### Security-utility frontier.

[Figure 4](#S7.F4 "In Models. ‣ 7.2 Evaluation ‣ 7 Implementation and Evaluation ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")
presents security and utility for each approach on both personas in our
dataset. Pincer achieves a significant jump in security while achieving
comparable utility to the baselines.
[Table 2](#S7.T2 "In Models. ‣ 7.2 Evaluation ‣ 7 Implementation and Evaluation ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")
shows the conditional rates strongly agreeing with this overall trend.

Figure 5: ASR by attack type. Solid bars are ASR; the wider faint bars
behind them are cASR. NanoClaw doesn’t have resource access gate, so its
cASR is omitted.

#### Comparison across attack types.

[Figure 5](#S7.F5 "In Security-utility frontier. ‣ 7.2 Evaluation ‣ 7 Implementation and Evaluation ‣ Pincer: Resource Authorization for Agents using a Digital Twin")
breaks ASR down by attack type for both personas. Across all attack
types, Pincer outperforms the majority of the baselines. Moreover, if we
focus on memory poisoning (MP), we observe a significant improvement
especially compared to Dynamic-Judge where the judge maintains its own
state and refers to it on each resource request (similar to the twin’s
state in Pincer); however, that state isn’t isolated in Dynamic-Judge.
The most striking result is for the provenance-laundering (PL) attack, a
type of misleading filename attack, where Pincer offers significantly
more protection than all baselines for both personas across the two LLM
model families (Haiku and Muse Spark).

#### Costs.

We found the token cost of all baselines to be significantly larger than
the undefended NanoClaw at around 2-5$`\times`$, while Pincer incurs an
additional 2-3$`\times`$ on top. While these costs may appear quite
large, there are several ways to bring them down significantly to the
point that the overhead of Pincer will be in a similar range to the
baselines and even further push the cost of all approaches closer to
NanoClaw. First, about half of the cost in Pincer is from reasoning
tokens of the twin because we haven’t explored routine compaction of its
state into standing policies in our implementation yet; it reasons
through its entire state on each request which causes a lot of
redundancy. Second, the number of LLM API calls in Pincer is bloated
signficantly because our resource request tool doesn’t implement batched
requests. Therefore, if the worker wants five resources, it has to stop
five times in a sequence requesting one resource at a time, and the twin
will reason about each from scratch. Lastly, for established tasks, the
twin can pre-approve resources like pre-committed policies () which can
be enforced via path matching similar to Conseca+.
````
